what: The detective note says vet's column 29 points at &err, but column 29 of line 17 is the %w verb. &err starts at column 34.
evidence: Page: "Line 17, column 29 is the &err. Fix: wrap err itself." Captured vet stderr: "wrap_ptr.go:17:29: %w wants operand of error type DiskFull, not pointer type *DiskFull (defeats errors.Is)". Source line 17 is '\treturn fmt.Errorf("backup: %w", &err)'. Counted with the tab as column 1, characters 29-30 are "%w" and '&' is column 34. Go 1.27.3's printf analyzer reports the range of the format directive: pass.ReportRangef(rng, "%%w wants operand ...") in src/cmd/vendor/golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/printf/printf.go:985.
fix: "Line 17, column 29 is the %w verb in the format string; the operand it complains about is &err, a little further along. Fix: wrap err itself."

what: The panel says Go's own encoding/json uses panic and recover inside. That is not true of the Go 1.27.3 build the page shows: its encoding/json is built on v2 by default and contains no recover.
evidence: Page: "Go's own encoding/json works like this inside." In Go 1.27.3, src/internal/buildcfg/exp.go sets the baseline experiment JSONv2: true. encode.go, the only non-test file with recover(), starts with //go:build !goexperiment.jsonv2. `go list -f '{{.GoFiles}}' encoding/json` on 1.27.3 lists only v2_decode.go, v2_encode.go, v2_indent.go, v2_inject.go, v2_options.go, v2_scanner.go and v2_stream.go. None of the v2 files calls recover(). text/template still does it: errRecover in src/text/template/exec.go turns its internal panics back into errors.
fix: "Go's own text/template works like this inside (and encoding/json did, up to Go 1.26)."

what: The boss parsons teaches wrapping err unconditionally: `err = fmt.Errorf("reading orders: %w", err)` runs even when ReadFile succeeded, so err is never nil on the happy path. The explanation hides this.
evidence: boss_parsons.go lines 11-13: `_, err := os.ReadFile("missing.txt")`, `err = fmt.Errorf("reading orders: %w", err)`, `if errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist) {`. Explain: "The last line runs only when the file exists." Re-run in a scratch copy with missing.txt present and err printed: "orders loaded; err = reading orders: %!w(<nil>) nil? false". A chapter whose catchphrase is "handle it once" should not model wrapping a nil error. Any later `if err != nil` would report a failure that never happened.
fix: Wrap only on failure: `if err != nil { err = fmt.Errorf("reading orders: %w", err) }` (pin the braces if needed), or return early. Then add one sentence to the explanation: wrap only when err != nil, because %w of nil gives a non-nil error that prints %!w(<nil>).

what: Two version claims in the Lab are slightly off. errors.AsType compiles with Go 1.27 in a go 1.25 module; only vet objects. And Go 1.27's vet pointer-wrap check also needs a go.mod that says go 1.27.
evidence: Page: "errors.AsType, which needs Go 1.26 and a go.mod that says go 1.26 or later. Go 1.27's vet is needed for the pointer-wrap check." Scratch module with `go 1.25` running custom.go on go1.27.3: go run printed all three lines and exited 0. go vet said "main.go:33:22: errors.AsType requires go1.26 or later (module is go1.25)". The same module with `go 1.26` and wrap_ptr.go: go vet on 1.27.3 printed nothing and exited 0. The analyzer is gated on versions.AtLeast(fileVersion, versions.Go1_27) (printf.go:979).
fix: "errors.AsType needs Go 1.26 or later (with an older go line, go vet warns). The pointer-wrap check needs Go 1.27's vet and a go.mod that says go 1.27 or later."

what: The caption quotes the buggy output so the reader can "see the spaces", but it is in an inline <samp>, which collapses the three inner spaces and the two trailing spaces to one each.
evidence: HTML: `<samp>"[STAMPED]   parcel 42  "</samp>` with the caption "%q prints the result in quotes so you can see the spaces". comic.css gives samp no white-space rule, so it renders as "[STAMPED] parcel 42 ". The terminal above shows the real spacing.

what: The bubble says a pre-release version "is never picked unless you ask for it". That overstates it: @latest falls back to the newest pre-release when a module has no release, and a dependency's requirement can pull a pre-release into the build.
evidence: "a dash adds a pre-release tag, like v1.5.0-beta.1, which comes before v1.5.0 and is never picked unless you ask for it." The Go Modules Reference (version queries) says @latest picks the highest release version, or else the highest pre-release if there are no releases. Under MVS, any require line can name a pre-release.
fix: "... which comes before v1.5.0, and @latest skips it while a normal release exists."
